title:
An AI requirement
that can't *fail*
can't be validated.
sub: Most AI requirements are aspirations wearing the word "shall".

title: You've probably written this one:
text:
"The system shall accurately extract data from batch records."

Nothing in that sentence can fail. So nothing in it can be tested — and the tester finds that out during execution, under deadline.

title: Why it happens:
text:
Nobody knows what number to write. And writing a number feels like committing to something you might miss.

So the requirement stays vague — and the decision quietly moves downstream to whoever is holding the script at 6pm.

title: Can this requirement fail?
text: If you can't describe the observable outcome that counts as failure, you don't have a requirement. You have an intention.

title:
What a testable AI
requirement needs:
items: *The threshold* — a number, and a reason for it
*The conditions* — which data, which population, which document type
*The evidence* — how pass and fail get recorded
*The owner* — who decides, before anyone runs it

title: Before → After
text:
~The system shall accurately extract data from batch records.~

*≥98% field-level accuracy against a 200-record human-adjudicated reference set. No single field below 95%. Re-measured at qualification and at every model change.*

title: Before → After
text:
~AI output shall be reviewed by a qualified user.~

*100% of Tier 3 outputs reviewed by a named role before entering the record. Reviewer disagreement rate monitored — a sustained rate below 2% triggers an automation-bias investigation.*

title:
That second one matters more
than it looks.
text:
If your reviewers never disagree with the model, they aren't reviewing it.

"Human in the loop" only becomes a control the moment it can fail.

title:
The hardest part is
the *threshold*.
text:
Here's the move nobody makes: measure what your current process actually achieves.

If your human reviewers catch 94%, then debating in the abstract whether 97% is "good enough" misses that you already accepted 94% — and never wrote it down.

title:
Setting the number *is*
the risk assessment.
text:
To choose a threshold you have to say what happens when it's wrong, who catches it, and what it costs.

That's the conversation everyone says they want and then skips — because it's easier to write "accurately".

title:
Has your org started the
AI-in-GxP journey?
text:
Forward this to your QA, CSV or IT lead — especially if requirements are being drafted right now.
